clinicalPearls: Prototype autoimmune disease defined by lymphocytic infiltration of exocrine glands causing xerostomia and dry eyes (keratoconjunctivitis sicca), together with marked B-cell hyperactivity.
Strongly female-predominant (female-to-male ratio roughly 10–20:1) and chiefly affects middle-aged women, but can present at any age including childhood; prevalence is approximately 0.5–1%.
Earlier age at onset tends to mark a more aggressive phenotype with more systemic manifestations and more serum autoantibodies.

Can occur alone or in association with other systemic rheumatic diseases, most commonly rheumatoid arthritis, limited scleroderma, and systemic lupus erythematosus; 5–20% of patients with other autoimmune diseases can have sicca features.

Principal oral symptom is dryness (xerostomia) with difficulty swallowing dry food, burning mouth, increased dental caries; examination may show dry erythematous sticky mucosa, atrophic tongue papillae, and a deeply fissured tongue.
Intermittent or persistent enlargement of the parotid or other major salivary glands occurs in about two-thirds of patients.

Ocular involvement classically produces a sandy or gritty sensation under the lids, with burning, stranded secretions at the inner canthi, reduced tearing, redness, and photosensitivity from corneal and conjunctival epithelial destruction (keratoconjunctivitis sicca).
Extraglandular (systemic) manifestations occur in about one-third of patients and are categorized as nonspecific, periepithelial, immune complex–mediated, and lymphoma.

Carries the highest risk of lymphoma among all autoimmune diseases; most are extranodal, low-grade, marginal zone (MALT) B-cell lymphomas, often found incidentally on labial minor salivary gland biopsy.
Most patients (about two-thirds) have an elevated ESR, hypergammaglobulinemia, antinuclear antibodies, rheumatoid factor, and anti-Ro52/Ro60 and anti-La autoantibodies.
The disease course is usually slow and benign in the majority of patients; antecedent major stressful life events have been reported prior to onset.
Recently described as triggerable by PD-1/PD-L1 checkpoint inhibitor therapy.
harrison.pathophysiology: Activated T lymphocytes are the major infiltrating cells in affected exocrine (chiefly salivary and lacrimal) glands, with B-cell populations prevailing in heavily infiltrated labial minor salivary gland tissue; follicular, myeloid, and plasmacytoid dendritic cells and macrophages are also present, the latter (with inflammasome activation) being linked to lymphoma risk. Ductal and acinar epithelial cells play an active pathogenic role: they aberrantly express costimulatory molecules and surface Ro/La autoantigens, secrete proinflammatory cytokines and lymphocyte-attracting chemokines that support ectopic germinal center formation, express innate-immunity Toll-like receptors (TLR3, 7, 9), and display immunoregulatory molecules (ICAM, CD40). Epithelial cells produce B cell–activating factor (BAFF), induced by type I and II interferons, and circulating BAFF is elevated (especially with hypergammaglobulinemia and autoantibodies), exerting an antiapoptotic effect on B lymphocytes; epithelial cells themselves show increased apoptosis. Disease initiation and perpetuation reflect interplay of endogenous triggers (intracellular stress, inappropriate expression of endogenous nucleic acids) and exogenous triggers (viruses, hormonal factors, stressful life events) on a genetically hyperactive immune background. Established genetic loci include HLA-DQA1*0501, interferon/BAFF axis variants (IRF5, STAT4, BAFF), B-cell function genes (EBF1, BLK), and combined deficiencies of the classical complement pathway.
additionalDifferentials: Sarcoidosis (granulomatous salivary gland infiltration, no Ro/La antibodies)
Diabetes mellitus and other metabolic causes of dry mouth/parotid enlargement
Marginal zone (MALT) B-cell lymphoma complicating the disease
infectionMimics: HIV infection with diffuse infiltrative lymphocytosis / sicca syndrome (young males, CD8+ glandular infiltrates, lacks anti-Ro/La, positive HIV serology)
Viral parotitis (mumps, influenza, Epstein-Barr virus, coxsackievirus A, cytomegalovirus)
nonInfectiousMimics: Diabetes mellitus, hyperlipoproteinemia (types IV and V), chronic pancreatitis, hepatic cirrhosis
Stevens-Johnson syndrome, pemphigoid, chronic conjunctivitis/blepharitis, hypovitaminosis A (dry eye)
additionalInvestigations: Schirmer’s I test for tear flow (≤5 mm/5 min on at least one eye supports diagnosis)
Tear breakup time or tear lysozyme content for tear composition
Slit-lamp examination after lissamine green or Rose Bengal staining; ocular staining score ≥5 or van Bijsterveld score ≥4
Sialometry / unstimulated whole saliva flow rate (≤0.1 mL/min supportive)
Salivary gland ultrasound (emerging diagnostic and prognostic tool); MRI and magnetic resonance sialography
Labial minor salivary gland biopsy with focus score ≥1 (foci per 4 mm2)

Serum autoantibodies: anti-Ro52/Ro60, anti-La, rheumatoid factor, ANA; anticentromere (limited scleroderma–like), antimitochondrial (autoimmune cholangitis), anti-21-hydroxylase (blunted adrenal response), anti-citrullinated peptide (arthritis), anticalponin-3 (peripheral neuropathy)
Complement (low C4), serum protein electrophoresis, cryoglobulins, serum IgG4, thyroid autoantibodies
Testing to exclude chronic viral infection (HCV, HIV) and chest x-ray to exclude sarcoidosis
FDG-PET/CT to help exclude lymphoma when suspected
redFlags: Parotid or major salivary gland enlargement, especially persistent or with a lymph node mass >7 cm — concern for lymphoma
Palpable purpura, urticarial lesions, skin ulcerations, or mononeuritis multiplex (immune complex–mediated vasculitis)
Low C4 complement, monoclonal gammopathy (paraproteinemia), and cryoglobulins — lymphoma risk markers
Heavy focal lymphocytic infiltrates with germinal center formation on salivary biopsy — lymphoma risk
Severe tongue atrophy and leukopenia in the appropriate context
Membranoproliferative glomerulonephritis with mixed type II/III cryoglobulinemia
Myelitis with anti-aquaporin-4 antibodies (rare CNS involvement)
harrison.prognosis: The disease usually evolves slowly and follows a benign course in most patients. The dominant adverse outcome is malignant transformation: Sjögren’s disease carries the highest lymphoma risk of any autoimmune disease, with clinical (parotid enlargement, severe tongue atrophy, palpable purpura), hematologic/serologic (leukopenia, autoantibodies, low C4, monoclonal gammopathy, cryoglobulins), and histopathologic (germinal center formation, heavy focal lymphocytic infiltrates) risk factors. Survival is reduced in patients with B symptoms, lymph node mass >7 cm, and high or intermediate histologic grade. Patients also have an increased risk of cardiovascular disease, paralleling rheumatoid arthritis and SLE.
pitfalls: Failing to take a careful medication history — diuretics, antihypertensives, anticholinergics, and antidepressants can themselves cause dryness and mimic or worsen sicca.
Overlooking HIV- or HCV-associated sicca syndrome, which can closely resemble Sjögren’s but lacks anti-Ro/La and has distinct demographics and glandular infiltrate phenotype.
Missing renal tubular dysfunction: interstitial nephritis may be asymptomatic, presenting only as hyposthenuria or renal tubular acidosis, and untreated acidosis can progress to nephrocalcinosis.
Attributing all salivary gland enlargement to benign disease and missing an incidental MALT lymphoma on labial biopsy.
Not excluding sarcoidosis, amyloidosis, IgG4-related disease, graft-versus-host disease, and prior head/neck radiation before diagnosing Sjögren’s disease.
Assuming arthritis is erosive — arthritis in primary Sjögren’s disease is characteristically nonerosive (may lead to Jaccoud’s arthropathy).
harrison.severityClassification: Diagnosis/classification per the 2016 ACR-EULAR criteria: suspect in patients with dry eyes and/or dry mouth (or systemic features such as major salivary gland enlargement, fatigue, Raynaud’s, small-joint arthralgia/arthritis, palpable purpura/urticaria, renal tubular acidosis/membranoproliferative GN, ILD/small airway disease, autoimmune cholangitis, peripheral neuropathy, or MS-like lesions), supported by objective findings: unstimulated whole saliva flow ≤0.1 mL/min, Schirmer’s test ≤5 mm/5 min, ocular staining score ≥5 (or van Bijsterveld ≥4), serum anti-Ro antibodies, and minor salivary gland biopsy focus score ≥1. Exclusions include prior head/neck radiation, active HCV, AIDS, sarcoidosis, amyloidosis, graft-versus-host disease, and IgG4-related disease. Extraglandular disease severity is gauged by the categories of involvement (nonspecific, periepithelial, immune complex–mediated, and lymphoma).
management: Relieve dry eyes with ocular surface lubricants and topical anti-inflammatory therapy such as topical ciclosporin, and dry mouth with saliva substitutes and muscarinic secretagogues such as pilocarpine or cevimeline
Institute meticulous dental care with topical fluoride and regular dental review to counter caries from xerostomia, and treat oral candidiasis promptly

Treat systemic and extraglandular disease with hydroxychloroquine for arthralgia and fatigue, escalating to corticosteroids and immunosuppressants such as methotrexate or azathioprine, and rituximab for refractory manifestations
Maintain lifelong surveillance for B-cell lymphoma, investigating persistent parotid enlargement, new lymphadenopathy, cryoglobulinaemia or unexplained cytopenias
Advise general measures including environmental humidification, saliva stimulation with sugar-free gum and avoidance of anticholinergic and drying medications
Provide multidisciplinary care with rheumatology, ophthalmology and oral medicine
